newsitem.title: CHINA: China president to sign troop cut pact with Russia.
newsitem.headline: China president to sign troop cut pact with Russia.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin is to visit Moscow in April to sign a pact to reduce troops along China's border with Russia and three central Asian states, Premier Li Peng said on Friday.
Jiang, who met Russian President Boris Yeltsin in China last April, would sign the troop reduction agreement with Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, Li said.
"China and Russia, the two sides will, together with the three Central Asian nations, sign a border troop reduction agreement," Li told a news briefing.
The pact would help the cause of peace and goodwill in the region, Li said.
"With the signing of this agreement, the border we share with the four nations will be a border of cooperation and good-neighbourliness," he said.
China and Russia clashed along their border in the 1960s when the two nuclear powers were at odds, and border disputes between the five countries have been long-standing.

Beijing and Moscow, once arch-rivals for leadership of the communist world, have been building steadily warmer and closer ties for the last decade and relations have improved even more quickly since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
"We hope our two countries can have a friendly relationship that is characterised by good-neighbourliness," Li said.

Li's emphasis on further improvement in once chilly Sino-Russian ties appeared to reflect Beijing's bid to use its relations with Russia as a counter to slowly warming ties with the United States, western diplomats said.
Jiang's visit, scheduled for April, would also focus on boosting trade ties between China and Russia, he said, adding that the economies of the two regional giants were complementary.
Li has said he hoped to see annual trade with Russia hit $8 to $10 billion this year and $20 billion by the end of the century.

Jiang played host to Yeltsin last April in China, where the two leaders participated in the signing of a confidence-building accord between the five countries aimed at reducing tensions along their mutual borders.
That pact bars the nations from holding military exercises aimed at each other and requires them to inform each other on the scope of exercises.
Basic agreement on the demarcation of the 4,300 km (2,671 mile) Sino-Russian border, the major border in the highly volatile region, was finally reached in 1991.

Li travelled to Moscow last December as part of what Beijing and Moscow hail as a new strategic partnership, but both sides say they have ruled out a revival of the close military and political alliance that existed in the 1950s.
